blocks: Select clips or a time range and press Cmd/Ctrl+up/down arrow to swap in the same span from the next or previous non-empty take. On a take lane the selection moves with it.
In Draw Mode, click and drag across a take to copy it to the main lane in one gesture, or click a take to fill a main-lane time selection from it.
Main-lane clips are independent copies, so either can be edited without changing the other. Take clips edit like any Arrangement clip and can be copied or dragged to Session slots.
Create Fades on Clip Edges (Record, Warp & Launch Settings) adds 4 ms crossfades between adjacent clips to prevent clicks; Cmd+Option+F / Ctrl+Alt+F adds them by hand.
Take material used in the main lane's comp is highlighted in the track colour; unused material is desaturated. Highlights only show when position and clip properties match.
Drag the edge of a highlight to move the split point between two adjacent parts of the comp.
Splitting recorded audio into separate stems such as vocals, drums and bass.
Stem separation splits recorded audio — a song, loop or sample — into parts you can warp, chop, rearrange and process like any audio clip.
Uses include isolating vocals for remixes, pulling apart melodies and rhythms, sampling single instruments, and blending stems in DJ mixes.
22.1 How Stem Separation Works in Live
Separation analyses the spectral and time characteristics of a signal and extracts the parts it detects as stems.
22.1 How Stem Separation Works in Live
Live uses a deep learning model trained for source separation that runs locally, with no internet connection or extra tools.
22.1 How Stem Separation Works in Live
Any mono or stereo file splits into four stems: Vocals, Drums, Bass and Others (everything else).
22.1 How Stem Separation Works in Live
Choose Separate Stems to New Audio Tracks from the context menu or Create menu, on a file in the browser or a clip in either view.
toggles pick which of the four stems to make;
Merge to Single Track combines two or three chosen stems into one;
the quality selector picks High Speed or High Quality;
Separate starts the process and stops playback.
Each stem gets its own track inside a new Group Track, coloured to match the dialog's toggles; the group takes the source track's colour. A single stem, or a merged one, goes on one track instead.
Only the clip's audible region is processed — between its start and end markers, or from the start marker through the loop of a looped warped clip.
In the Arrangement, Separate Stems for Time Selection on a clip splits it at the selection's edges and separates only that part.
Source track effects move to the Group Track; track automation is copied to the group, and clip envelopes and modulation to each stem clip.
The source clip is deactivated to avoid doubling; select it and press 0 to turn it back on.
From the browser, stems land in whichever view has focus. In an empty Set with warping on for samples, the Set tempo follows the source.

Files go to the Project's Samples/Processed/Stems folder (merged stems keep their individual files too), in the File Type from the Record, Warp & Launch Settings, at 44.1 kHz and the source's bit depth.
High Speed separates every stem in one pass. It can still take several minutes on older computers.
High Quality gives cleaner results (a higher signal-to-distortion ratio) by running separate passes for Vocals, Drums and Bass, then deriving Others from what remains.
Crop the clip first to save time: Crop Clip Sample to Time Selection in the Sample Editor, or Crop Clip in the Arrangement, both Cmd+Shift+J (Mac) / Ctrl+Shift+J (Windows).
In High Quality, choosing fewer stems saves time unless Others is included, since Others needs all three other passes. Unused stems from those passes are still saved in the Stems folder.
Older Windows computers and Intel Macs separate on the CPU only, so they're slower than Apple silicon Macs, which also use the GPU.
Some sounds land in an unexpected stem, such as hi-hat highs in Others or chorused synths in Vocals. Trying both modes can show which suits the material.
The Device View and how MIDI effects, instruments and audio effects sit in a track's device chain, including delay compensation.
Every track can hold devices of three kinds:
MIDI effects — work on MIDI; MIDI tracks only.
Every track can hold devices of three kinds:
Audio effects — work on audio; audio, return and Main tracks, or MIDI tracks after an instrument.
Every track can hold devices of three kinds:
Instruments — take MIDI in and put audio out; MIDI tracks only.
Every track can hold devices of three kinds:

Individual devices are described in Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference, Ableton/Live/UG/30 MIDI Effect Reference and Ableton/Live/UG/31 Instrument Reference; grouping them is covered in Ableton/Live/UG/25 Racks; sharing one device across tracks through returns is in Ableton/Live/UG/17 Routing and IO.
The Device View at the bottom of the window shows the selected track's devices; double-click a track's title bar to open it.
Normally Clip View and Device View take turns. The toggles next to their selectors at the bottom right stack Clip View above Device View so both stay open.
Cmd+Option+3 / Cmd+Option+4 (Mac) or Ctrl+Alt+3 / Ctrl+Alt+4 (Windows) show or hide Clip View and Device View.
Double-click a device's title bar, or choose Fold, to collapse it.
The browser sidebar has labels for Live's devices, Max for Live devices and plug-ins.

Double-click a device to add it to the selected track (or a new track), select it and press Enter, or drag it to a track, a drop area or the Device View. Dropping a sample into a MIDI track's Device View creates a with it.

With Auto monitoring, a track must be armed to hear an external input through its devices; adding an instrument to a MIDI track usually arms it. See Ableton/Live/UG/17 Routing and IO/01 Monitoring for other setups.
Signals run left to right, so order matters. In a MIDI track, everything before the instrument is MIDI and everything after is audio, so a chain can go MIDI effects → instrument → audio effects.

Select a device's title bar and press Delete to remove it; drag title bars to reorder, or into another track to move. Cut, copy, paste and duplicate work too; pasted devices go before the selected one, or at the end if you click after the last device. Changes don't interrupt the audio.
Meters between devices show where a signal drops out or gets too hot.
There's no clipping between devices; it only happens at physical outputs or in rendered files.
Clip envelopes can automate or modulate device parameters per clip; see Ableton/Live/UG/27 Clip Envelopes.

The title bar turns the device on and off, saves and hot-swaps presets, saves defaults and opens the context menu. Some devices add controls, such as a scale awareness toggle or the Chord device's Learn toggle.
The Activator toggle switches a device off as if removed: the signal passes untouched and it uses no CPU. Freezing tracks helps with heavy devices.
An arrow next to the Activator opens a view above the Device View, such as Roar's Gain Stage and Modulation Matrix or EQ Eight's frequency display.
A triangle in the title bar expands a view inside the device, such as Phaser-Flanger's LFO and Envelope Follower.
Right-click the title bar or use the Show Options toggle for the context menu: general commands like Cut, Copy and Rename, plus device-specific ones such as Auto Filter's Mono Sidechain.
Every built-in device holds two states, A and B, with separate parameter values, for comparing edits — useful for presets, EQ and compression.
On loading, A and B are the same. Edits go to A while B keeps the starting values.
Compare: Copy A to B (Edit menu, context menu or Show Options) copies values across; Compare: Switch to B, or P, switches state. The title bar shows "(B)" while B is active.
Not available for Racks, Max for Live devices or plug-ins.
Automation belongs to one state: switching disables it, and switching back doesn't re-enable it. Use Re-Enable Automation in the parameter's context menu in the state you want.
Copying a device, or saving it as a preset, takes only the active state's values and uses them for both A and B.
Max for Live can reach the states through the Live API.

Each device shows as a folder in the browser's content pane. The folder itself is the default preset (factory or your own default); the presets inside have custom settings. Presets come from the Core Library, Packs, or your own saves.
Browse with the arrow keys: up and down to move, left and right to close and open folders, Enter to load onto the selected track. Double-click or drag also work.
Live device files (Ableton/File/.adg, Ableton/File/.adv, Ableton/File/.amxd) can be dragged in from Finder or Explorer, though the browser is preferred.
Drop a preset over an existing one in a device chain to replace it.
Hot-Swap links a device to the browser so you can audition and load other presets in its place. Press Q or click the Hot-Swap Presets button in the title bar.
Q swaps the selected device, or else the first audio effect on an audio track or the instrument on a MIDI track.

The browser opens at the device's folder. Any preset of the same device type can be swapped in — an audio effect can't be swapped for a MIDI effect. Arrow keys browse; Enter or double-click loads. Load the parent folder for the device's default settings.
Adding -EnableHotSwapOnSelection to Options.txt loads each preset as soon as it's selected.
Leave with Q, Esc, the X in the browser's Hot-Swap bar or in the title bar, or by moving to another view.

Drum Rack pads, Drum Sampler, Impulse, Sampler and Simpler have a Hot-Swap Sample button: bottom right of each pad, of Drum Sampler's waveform, of each Impulse slot and of Simpler's sample display; top left of Sampler's expanded Zone Editor. Except in Sampler, it appears only on hover.
It opens the sample's folder in the browser; load another with Enter or double-click.
Leave by clicking the button again, the X in the Hot-Swap bar, Esc, Q, or moving to another view.
The Save Preset button in the title bar saves the current settings, and any Info View text, as a new preset in the User Library's Presets folder. Name it and press Enter, or Esc to cancel.
Dragging a device by its title bar into any folder under Places saves it there.
If Collect Files on Export (Library Settings) is set to Ask, saving a preset that uses samples asks whether to copy them.
More in Ableton/Live/UG/04 Browser and, for Project-specific presets, Ableton/Live/UG/05 Managing Files and Sets.
Defaults apply your most-used settings automatically. They can:
load devices with set parameter values;
Defaults apply your most-used settings automatically. They can:
load VST and Audio Units plug-ins with set parameter configurations;
Defaults apply your most-used settings automatically. They can:
create audio and MIDI tracks with set devices and mixer settings;
Defaults apply your most-used settings automatically. They can:
choose the presets used for dropping samples, slicing and converting audio to MIDI.
Defaults apply your most-used settings automatically. They can:
They live in the User Library's Defaults folder. Delete one from its context menu, or select it and press Delete, to return to factory settings.

Set a device up and choose Save as Default Preset from its Options or context menu (instruments, MIDI and audio effects, and Racks). It is saved under Defaults in Audio Effects, Instruments or MIDI Effects, and loads every time the device is added — samples included for instruments.
Dragging a device into those folders works too, as long as it keeps the device's own name, such as "Simpler". Saving a new default asks before overwriting.

For a VST or Audio Units plug-in, add parameters in Configure Mode and choose Save as Default Configuration. It is saved to Plug-In Configurations → Audio Units or VSTs; VST and AU versions can have separate defaults.
Only the list of parameters is saved, not their values. To keep values too, put the plug-in in a Rack and save the Rack as a default preset.

Set up a track's devices and mixer settings (routing, volume, pan, sends) and choose Save as Default Audio Track or Save as Default MIDI Track from its title bar's context menu. It goes to Creating Tracks → Audio Track or MIDI Track and applies to every new track of that kind.
Dragging a track there also works if it is named Default Audio Track or Default MIDI Track.

To choose the instrument made when a sample is dropped into an empty MIDI track's Device View or onto a Drum Rack pad, set up an empty Sampler or Simpler and drag it to Dropping Samples → On Device View or On Drum Rack. A pad's Save as Default Pad adds to On Drum Rack too.
If a folder holds several, the last one added is used.

Build an empty Drum Rack with one chain holding an empty Sampler or Simpler, plus any effects and Macro mappings, and drag it into the Slicing folder. It then appears in the Slicing Preset chooser of Slice to New MIDI Track; see Ableton/Live/UG/13 Audio to MIDI.

Custom Racks for Harmony, Melody and Drums to MIDI go in the matching Audio to MIDI folder. Use an Instrument Rack (or a single instrument) for Harmony and Melody; Drums needs a top-level Drum Rack with Sampler or Simpler on its pads, not one nested in an Instrument Rack.
If a folder holds several, the last one added is used.

A Defaults folder, with the same subfolders, inside the Current Project overrides the User Library defaults for Sets in that Project. Create folders in Finder/Explorer or with New Folder in the browser, then drag devices or tracks in.

Plug-ins can't be dragged into the Project. Instead, create Plug-In Configurations/Audio Units and VSTs folders there, save a configuration as usual, and move its folder with the Default.appc file from the User Library into the Project.
The Save as Default menu commands always save to the User Library, not the Project.
Live compensates automatically for processing delays from built-in devices and plug-ins, return tracks included, keeping tracks in sync with as little delay as possible between playing and hearing.
It's on by default; Options → Delay Compensation turns it off.

With it on, Reduced Latency When Monitoring (Options menu) skips compensation on input-monitored tracks for the lowest latency, at the risk of those tracks falling out of sync with compensated ones such as returns.
Tempo-synced effects placed after delay-causing devices can sound out of time.

Very large track delays or plug-in latencies can make Live sluggish. Turning compensation off is not usually advised and also disables Track Delay; adjusting track delays may help instead. Compensation can add CPU load.
Using VST and Audio Units plug-ins in Live and their sidechain inputs.
Plug-ins extend Live's devices. Live supports VST2, VST3, Audio Units 2 and Audio Units 3 (AU on macOS only, AU3 from Live 11.2).
Plug-ins behave like Live devices: instruments go on MIDI tracks, effects on audio tracks or after instruments; see Ableton/Live/UG/23 Instruments and Effects.

Plug-ins appear under the browser's Plug-Ins label, instruments with a keyboard icon. Only Audio Units presets show in the browser, and some AU factory presets appear only once the device is on a track with Hot-Swap on.
On first launch the Plug-Ins label is empty until plug-in sources are activated (see the VST and Audio Units sections below).
Hold Option (Mac) / Alt (Windows) while Live starts to skip the plug-in scan, which helps find a plug-in that crashes Live.
Plug-ins installed or removed while Live runs appear after a restart, or after Rescan in the Plug-Ins Settings. Option/Alt+Rescan deletes the plug-in database and scans from scratch.
Intel Macs can't run PowerPC-only plug-ins.
A plug-in with up to 64 parameters shows them all as sliders in a Live panel. One with more opens with an empty panel to configure.
The unfold button in the title bar shows or hides the parameters.
The X-Y field controls two parameters at once, chosen in the menus beneath it, which suits live performance.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
The Show/Hide Plug-In Window button opens the plug-in's own interface in a floating window, kept in sync with the Live panel.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
Auto-Open Plug-In Windows — open the window when a plug-in is loaded from the browser.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
Multiple Plug-In Windows — allow several open at once; otherwise hold Cmd (Mac) / Ctrl (Windows) while opening to keep earlier ones.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
Auto-Hide Plug-In Windows — show only the selected track's windows.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows
View → Show/Hide Plug-In Windows, or Cmd+Option+P (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+P (Windows), hides and shows windows already opened. Each window's title names its track.
24.1.1 Showing Plug-In Panels in Separate Windows

Configure in the device header lets you choose which parameters appear in Live's panel: click a control in the plug-in window to add it (some need their value changed; some plug-ins don't expose every parameter).

In Configure Mode, drag to reorder and press Delete to remove; Live warns before removing a parameter with automation, envelopes or mappings. Plug-ins without their own window can reorder but not delete.
The configuration is saved per instance in the Set. To reuse it, save the plug-in inside a Rack, or save it as a default configuration.
Parameters can also be added without Configure Mode:
tweaking a control in the plug-in window makes a temporary entry in the automation, clip envelope and X-Y choosers; editing or selecting it there makes it permanent;
Parameters can also be added without Configure Mode:
controls moved in the plug-in window while recording get automation and join the panel;
Parameters can also be added without Configure Mode:
in MIDI, key or Macro mapping mode, a control you move joins the panel, selected and ready to map.
Parameters can also be added without Configure Mode:
After that, a plug-in works like a Live device: MIDI mapping, moving and copying, clip envelopes, multiple I/O in track routing (Ableton/Live/UG/17 Routing and IO) and custom info text.
Sidechaining lets another signal trigger a plug-in's processing. Supported plug-ins show sidechain controls at the left of the device.
The choosers select any internal routing point as the trigger.
Gain sets the sidechain input level; Mix blends the trigger between sidechain (100%) and the plug-in's own input (0%). The sidechain is only a trigger and is never heard.
Mute plays only the plug-in's output, without the sidechain source.
Setting up VST plug-in folders, and using VST presets and banks.
VST sources must be activated before first use: press Activate in the browser's Plug-Ins panel, or open the Plug-Ins Settings with Cmd+, (Mac) / Ctrl+, (Windows) and find Plug-In Sources.
Windows: Browse to set the VST Plug-In Custom Folder (Live may already have found it in the registry) and turn on Use VST Plug-In Custom Folder.
macOS: plug-ins in /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST (home and local) are used when Use VST plug-ins in System Folders is on. A custom folder can be added alongside or instead, with its own on/off option.
Live scans the chosen folders and their subfolders. Aliases placed in a scanned folder can point to plug-ins elsewhere, even on another drive.
A plug-in that crashes the scan is reported on the next launch, with the choice to rescan or disable it. One that crashes twice is disabled until reinstalled.
Each VST instance owns a fixed-size bank of presets, chosen below the title bar. Edits always change the selected preset.
Unlike Live presets, which every instance and Set share, VST presets belong to that one instance.
Rename the current preset with Edit → Rename Plug-In Preset while the title bar is selected.

Load Preset or Bank imports a preset or bank file (on Windows choose the file type in the dialog). Save Preset or Bank saves the current preset or the whole bank, picking VST Preset or VST Bank as the format.
Audio Units run on macOS only and behave much like VST plug-ins.
To activate them, press Activate under the browser's Plug-Ins label, or turn on Use Audio Units in Plug-Ins Settings → Plug-In Sources.
Some AU plug-ins have device modes, such as reverb quality, set only in the plug-in's own window.
AU presets work like Live presets, though some are read-only and can't be moved in the browser. They are .aupreset files stored in (Home)/Library/Audio/Presets/(Manufacturer)/(Plug-in).
Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks: chains, zones, Macro Controls and mixing inside a Rack.

A Rack holds effects, plug-ins and instruments in a track's device chain. Racks can build complex processors, playable performance instruments and stacked synths, while gathering the most important controls in one place. Even a single device gains from a Rack, through new control relationships between its parameters.
How signals flow through a Rack's parallel chains, and what Macro Controls are.
25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains
A track's devices normally run in series, left to right, in one chain. A Rack adds parallel chains.
25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains
In Instrument and Effect Racks, every chain receives the same input at once, processes it through its own devices in series, and the chains' outputs are mixed into the Rack's output.
25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains
In a Drum Rack, each chain receives only its assigned MIDI note.
25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains
A whole Rack behaves as a single device: it can go anywhere in a chain, Racks can nest without limit, and devices after it receive its output.
25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains

Macro Controls are a bank of knobs, each able to control any number of parameters across the Rack's devices — to bring one parameter forward, to morph many at once, or to hide a complex instrument behind a small custom panel. See .
Mapping the Macros to a hardware controller makes them playable.
Four kinds of Rack, each with its own rules:
MIDI Effect Rack — MIDI effects only, on MIDI tracks.
Four kinds of Rack, each with its own rules:
Audio Effect Rack — audio effects only, on audio tracks or after an instrument on MIDI tracks.
Four kinds of Rack, each with its own rules:
Instrument Rack — instruments, plus MIDI effects before them and audio effects after.
Four kinds of Rack, each with its own rules:
Drum Rack — like an Instrument Rack, plus up to six return chains of audio effects with per-chain send levels. See Ableton/Instrument/Drum Rack.
Four kinds of Rack, each with its own rules:
Create an empty Rack by dragging a generic Rack preset (such as "Audio Effect Rack") from the browser, then drop devices into its Chain List or Devices view.

To wrap existing devices, select their title bars, right-click and choose Group (Cmd+G / Ctrl+G) or Group to Drum Rack. Grouping again, or grouping chains, nests a Rack inside a Rack; the Device View shows each level as a pair of brackets.
Ungroup on a Rack's title bar takes it apart.
A column at the Rack's left holds selectors for its views: Macro Controls, Chain List (with return chains in a Drum Rack), Devices, and the Drum Rack's Pad View.
Rounded corners bracket a Rack's contents; with Devices shown, the closing bracket moves to keep nesting clear.
Select a Rack by its own title bar to move, copy, delete, rename it, or edit its info text.
Hiding every view folds the Rack into its view column, the same as Fold or double-clicking its title bar.
Right-click the Device View selector for a list of every device in the track, nested Racks included; choose one to jump to it.

The Chain List is where incoming signals branch: each parallel chain is one entry. Drop presets, devices or whole chains into the area below to add chains. Racks, chains and devices drag freely between Racks and tracks; hovering over another track while dragging opens its Device View.
The selected chain is what the Devices view shows; arrow keys flip through chains. Several chains can be selected for copying and regrouping.
Each chain has an Activator, Solo and Hot-Swap. Instrument, Drum and Audio Effect Rack chains add volume and pan; Drum Rack chains add sends and MIDI note settings.
Chains save as presets in the browser, and can be renamed, given info text, or coloured from the context menu.
With Auto Select on, chains are selected as they process signal: in a Drum Rack, when their note arrives; in other Racks, according to their zones. Useful for troubleshooting.
Zones are filters at the input of each chain in Instrument and Effect Racks that decide which values reach it. They pass everything until you change them.

The Key, Vel and Chain buttons above the Chain List open their editors; Hide closes them. Audio Effect Racks have only chain select zones; Drum Racks have no zones and filter by note in the chain list.
Each zone has a lower bar to move or resize it and a thin upper bar for fade ranges. Drag edges to resize, the middle to move.
In a MIDI Effect Rack with four chains, all chains receive the same MIDI.
Before entering a chain, a note must pass that chain's key zone, then its velocity zone, then its chain select zone. Failing any one keeps it out.
The outputs of all chains are mixed and passed to whatever follows the Rack.
The Key Zone Editor shows each chain's range across the full MIDI note range, almost 11 octaves. Chains respond only to notes in their zone, which makes keyboard splits.
Fade ranges lower the velocity of notes entering the chain.
In Instrument and MIDI Effect Racks, each chain also responds only to a range of Note On velocities, 1–127, edited like key zones.
Fade ranges lower the velocity of notes entering the chain.
Chain select zones let one parameter, the draggable Chain selector above the 0–127 scale, choose which chains can play. Only chains whose zone overlaps the selector's value produce output.
In Instrument and MIDI Effect Racks they filter only notes by default; Chain Selector Filters MIDI Ctrl in the ruler's context menu makes them filter all MIDI.

In MIDI Effect Racks fades lower note velocity. In Instrument and Audio Effect Racks fades lower each chain's output volume: moving the selector off a zone that ends in a fade silences the chain, while a zone without a fade lets reverb tails and delays ring out.
25.5.4.1 Making Preset Banks Using Chain Select

Chain select zones default to a length of 1 at value 0. Place four chains with different effects at values 0, 1, 2 and 3 with no overlap, and map the Chain selector to a hardware encoder: turning it switches between four setups.
25.5.4.1 Making Preset Banks Using Chain Select
25.5.4.2 Crossfading Preset Banks Using Fade Ranges

Lengthen the zones and add fade ranges so neighbouring presets overlap, keeping one value where each plays alone. Moving the selector then crossfades between presets; wider fades make smoother transitions.
25.5.4.2 Crossfading Preset Banks Using Fade Ranges
Ableton/Instrument/Drum Racks share most features with other Racks but are laid out for drum kits.
Four extra toggles in the view column show the Input/Output, Send and Return sections and Auto Select.

Input/Output: Receive sets the incoming note the chain answers (with note names, numbers and General MIDI drum names); Play sets the note sent on to its devices; Choke puts it in one of sixteen choke groups, where triggering one chain silences the others, such as a closed hi-hat cutting an open one. With Receive on All Notes, Play and Choke are disabled. The Preview button fires a test note.
Mixer: besides volume, pan and Hot-Swap, each chain has post-fader sends to the return chains, once they exist.
Return chains: up to six chains of audio effects at the bottom of the list, fed by the sends. Each return's Audio To goes to the Rack's output or straight to the Set's return tracks.
Pad View shows one pad per MIDI note (128 in all). Shift the visible 16 pads by dragging in the overview or with the arrow keys; hold Cmd (Mac) / Alt (Windows) to move one row.

Drop almost anything from the browser on a pad and it maps to that note: a sample makes a chain with a ; an audio effect goes after it; another sample replaces only the Simpler and its sample, keeping effects. In Hot-Swap, D switches the target between the Rack and the last selected pad.
Dropping several samples maps them upward chromatically from the pad. Cmd/Alt-dragging them layers all on one pad in a nested Instrument Rack.

Dragging one pad onto another swaps their notes, so existing clips play different sounds; Cmd/Alt-dragging layers both pads. See also Ableton/How To/Preserve Name of Clip when Dragging into Drum Rack.
Receive choosers in the chain list remap notes too; chains sharing a note all fire from its pad.
A pad stands for a note, not a chain — every chain at any depth that receives that note:
an empty pad shows its note, and its General MIDI suggestion in the Status Bar;
A pad stands for a note, not a chain — every chain at any depth that receives that note:
a pad with one chain shows its name and gives mute, solo, preview, Hot-Swap, rename and delete;
A pad stands for a note, not a chain — every chain at any depth that receives that note:
a pad with several shows "Multi"; mute, solo, preview and delete affect them all.
A pad stands for a note, not a chain — every chain at any depth that receives that note:
With a natively supported pad controller selected in Settings → Link, Tempo & MIDI, its pads play the pads visible on screen and follow when you scroll.
A Rack can show up to 16 Macro Controls; new Racks show eight. Buttons in the view column add or remove visible Macros, and the count is saved with the Set.
The Map button in the Macro view turns on Macro Map Mode: mappable parameters get a coloured overlay, Map buttons appear under each Macro, and the Mapping Browser opens.
